summary: Defines how the entities in a Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain, the mobile access gateway and the local mobility anchor, interact with an AAA server using Diameter. The main use is downloading and updating per-device policy profiles from a remote policy store. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5779 lets the two Proxy Mobile IPv6 helpers, the access gateway and the mobility anchor, talk to a home Diameter server over Diameter. The server holds a rulebook for each mobile device, and the exchanges here fetch that rulebook and confirm that a device may use the mobility service.

subtitle: How Proxy Mobile IPv6 gateways and anchors ask a home AAA server for per-device rules and permission.

tldr.problem: In a Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain, each mobile device needs a policy profile: the rules that say how it may be served. Configuring those rules on every access gateway by hand does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the Diameter exchanges between the Mobile Access Gateway, the Local Mobility Anchor and the home AAA server, and the attribute value pairs that carry the policy profile, the assigned addresses and the capability flags.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard from February 2010 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines no new Diameter application or command code, so it plugs into existing Diameter deployments.

facts.label: Link-layer identifier encoding
facts.value: Upper-case ASCII octets separated by a hyphen, e.g. 00-23-32-C9-79-38

facts.label: New Diameter applications
facts.value: None; the RFC is generic to NASREQ and EAP

facts.label: Home network prefix rule
facts.value: The low 64 bits of the MIP6-Home-Link-Prefix must be all zeroes

today: RFC 5779 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2010, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes the Diameter exchanges used for Proxy Mobile IPv6 as they were defined at the time, and it deliberately adds no Diameter application or command code of its own.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 5779 defines the Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) interactions between a Mobile Access Gateway (MAG) and a AAA server, and between a Local Mobility Anchor (LMA) and a AAA server, inside a Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) domain. These interactions are primarily used to download and update mobile node specific policy profile information between the PMIPv6 entities and a remote policy store.

Downloading a policy profile to the gateway from a remote store is useful because it eases deployment and network maintenance in larger PMIPv6 domains. The same AAA infrastructure that authenticates and authorizes the mobile node for network access can be reused to fetch some or all of the policy profile the gateway needs.

After the network has authenticated the mobile node, the MAG sends a Proxy Binding Update (PBU) to the LMA to set up a mobility session on behalf of the mobile node. When the LMA receives the PBU, it may need to authorize that PBU against the AAA infrastructure. The same infrastructure is also used to update the remote policy store with mobility session information the LMA holds.

In this specification the home AAA server, called the HAAA, is co-located with the remote policy store. The Network Access Server (NAS) function may be co-located with the MAG function inside the network access router. Diameter, specified in RFC 3588, is the AAA protocol used.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC defines how a mobile device's gateway and mobility anchor talk to a central server over Diameter, the protocol used for sign-in and accounting. The main job is fetching the rules that apply to one device.

sections.title: The PMIPv6 Domain and Its Entities
sections.content:
A PMIPv6 domain has three kinds of entity. The Mobile Access Gateway sits at the edge of the access network and is the point where the mobile node attaches. The Local Mobility Anchor is the entity that holds the mobile node's home address and serves as the routing anchor for its traffic. The home AAA server holds the subscriber's records and, in this specification, also acts as the remote policy store.

Two separate Diameter interfaces connect the domain to the HAAA. The MAG-to-HAAA interface, marked (1) in the RFC's Figure 1, runs between each gateway and the HAAA. The LMA-to-HAAA interface, marked (2), runs between the anchor and the HAAA. The gateway reaches the anchor over an IPv4 or IPv6 network, and two tunnels, Tunnel1 and Tunnel2, carry the mobile node's traffic between the gateway and the anchor.

When a mobile node attaches, a network access authentication procedure usually starts. The choice of mechanism depends on the access network, and may be based on the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP). During that procedure the MAG, acting as a NAS, queries the HAAA using Diameter. If the HAAA finds that the subscriber is also authorized for the PMIPv6 service, PMIPv6 specific information is returned along with the successful authentication answer.

After the mobile node has been authenticated, the MAG sends a PBU to the LMA based on the node's policy profile information. On receiving the PBU, the LMA interacts with the HAAA and fetches the relevant parts of the subscriber policy profile and the authorization information related to the mobility service session.
sections.plainLanguage: Three parts take part: the gateway where the device connects, the anchor that holds its address, and a central server that holds the subscriber's records. The gateway and the anchor each open their own Diameter connection to that server, and the device's traffic travels between the gateway and the anchor over a pair of tunnels.

sections.title: The MAG-to-HAAA Interface
sections.content:
The MAG-to-HAAA interactions bootstrap the PMIPv6 mobility session when a mobile node attaches to a PMIPv6 domain and authenticates to it. The interface may also be used for accounting. The MAG acts as a Diameter client on this interface.

This specification defines no new Application-IDs or Command Codes for either Diameter connection. It is generic to any Diameter application and its commands that suits network access authentication and authorization, for example NASREQ from RFC 4005 and EAP from RFC 4072.

Whenever the MAG sends a Diameter request to the HAAA, the User-Name attribute value pair should carry the mobile node's identity, unless the identity is being suppressed for policy reasons, such as when identity hiding is in effect. The identity, when available, must be in Network Access Identifier (NAI) format. At minimum, the home realm of the mobile node must be available at the MAG when network access authentication takes place, because without it the MAG cannot route the Diameter request messages towards the correct HAAA.

The identity used on this interface may be entirely related to the network access authentication, and therefore not suitable as the mobile node identifier mobility option value in the later PBU and Proxy Binding Acknowledgement (PBA) messages. For session management and service authorization, session state should be maintained on the MAG-to-HAAA interface.
sections.plainLanguage: When a device connects, the gateway signs it in with the home server over Diameter. The gateway puts the device's name in the User-Name field so the server knows which subscriber record to look up, and it needs the device's home realm to find that server in the first place.

sections.title: The LMA-to-HAAA Interface
sections.content:
The LMA-to-HAAA interface has several uses: authorizing the incoming PBU, updating the LMA address at the HAAA, delegating assignment of the mobile node's home network prefix (MN-HNP) or IPv4 home address (IPv4-MN-HoA) to the HAAA, and handling accounting and PMIPv6 session management. Its primary purpose is to update the HAAA with the LMA address information in case of a dynamically assigned LMA, and to exchange mobile node address assignment information between the LMA and the HAAA.

Whenever the LMA sends a Diameter request, the User-Name attribute should carry the mobile node's identity, and that identity is strongly recommended to be the same as the mobile node identifier in the PBU mobility option. It should also match the identity used on the MAG-to-HAAA interface; where the two differ, the HAAA must have a mechanism to map one to the other. If the PBU carries a link-layer identifier, the Calling-Station-Id attribute should be included. If the PBU carries a service selection mobility option, the Service-Selection attribute should be included.

The Auth-Request-Type attribute must be set to AUTHORIZE_ONLY. If the HAAA cannot authorize the subscriber's mobility service session, the reply to the LMA must set the Result-Code attribute to DIAMETER_AUTHORIZATION_REJECTED (5003), which indicates a permanent failure. The failed authorization results in a rejected PBU, and a PBA with an appropriate error Status Value is sent back to the MAG.

Authorization must be performed at least for the initial PBU that sets up a mobility session. For later re-registration and handover PBUs the step may be repeated, in which case the interface should also maintain an authorization session state.

For address management, the LMA and the HAAA use the MIP6-Home-Link-Prefix attribute to exchange the MN-HNP and the PMIP6-IPv4-Home-Address attribute to exchange the IPv4-MN-HoA. Both sit inside the MIP6-Agent-Info attribute. Which entity owns address management is deployment specific and must be agreed per deployment. When the LMA owns it, the MIP6-Agent-Info attribute tells the HAAA which prefix or address was assigned. When the LMA delegates it to the HAAA, the request carries undefined addresses, that is 0::0 and 0.0.0.0, and the LMA expects the assigned values back in the answer.

The specification defines no HAAA-initiated LMA relocation. So when the MIP6-Agent-Info attribute appears in an answer from the HAAA to the LMA, the HAAA signals this by setting the MIP-Home-Agent-Address to the all zeroes address, for example 0::0, and leaving out the MIP-Home-Agent-Host attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: After the gateway asks the anchor to set up a session, the anchor asks the home server whether the device is allowed to have one. If the server says no, the request is refused with the error code 5003 and the gateway is told to fail the session. The same exchange is where the anchor tells the server which address it uses and which address the device was given.

sections.title: Attribute Value Pairs
sections.content:
Diameter carries information in attribute value pairs (AVPs). This section describes the AVPs this specification defines and the way it reuses existing ones in a PMIPv6 specific way. The MIP6-Agent-Info grouped AVP, code 486, defined in RFC 5447, carries the LMA addressing information and the MN-HNP. This specification extends it with the PMIP6-IPv4-Home-Address AVP, using the Diameter extensibility rules. The extended grouping has this form:

MIP6-Agent-Info ::= < AVP-Header: 486 > *2[ MIP-Home-Agent-Address ] [ MIP-Home-Agent-Host ] [ MIP6-Home-Link-Prefix ] [ PMIP6-IPv4-Home-Address ] * [ AVP ]

If the MIP-Home-Agent-Address is set to the all zeroes address, the receiver must ignore that attribute.

The PMIP6-IPv4-Home-Address AVP, code 505, is of type Address and holds an IPv4 address. It carries the IPv4-MN-HoA from the HAAA to the MAG and should only be present when the mobile node is statically provisioned with that address, because proactive dynamic assignment may reserve IPv4 address resources the node never uses. The MIP6-Home-Link-Prefix AVP, code 125, carries the MN-HNP; the low 64 bits of the prefix must be all zeroes. The PMIP6-DHCP-Server-Address AVP, code 504, holds the IP address of the DHCP server assigned to the gateway serving the newly attached mobile node, with the Address type matching whether it is a DHCPv4 or a DHCPv6 server address.

The Mobile-Node-Identifier AVP, code 506, is of type UTF8String and holds the mobile node identifier in NAI format. It is used on the MAG-to-HAAA interface for deployments where the gateway cannot find such an identity by other means, for example because of identity hiding, or where the HAAA wants to assign periodically changing identities. The gateway must use the received identifier if it has not obtained one by other means, and must silently discard it if it already holds a valid identifier.

The Calling-Station-Id AVP, code 31, holds a link-layer identifier of the mobile node, encoded in ASCII in upper case only with octet values separated by a hyphen, for example 00-23-32-C9-79-38. The Service-Selection AVP, code 493, holds a service identifier and is re-used from RFC 5778; the identifier must be unique within the PMIPv6 domain. The Service-Configuration AVP, code 507, is of type Grouped and carries a service and an LMA pair, so the HAAA can tell the gateway which services the node subscribes to and which LMAs host them.

The MIP6-Feature-Vector AVP, originally defined in RFC 5447, carries capability flags. This document adds three bits: PMIP6_SUPPORTED, which says the gateway supports PMIPv6 and which the HAAA mirrors back to say it supports PMIPv6 too; IP4_HOA_SUPPORTED, which says the gateway can act as a minimal DHCP server and relay and deliver an IPv4 home address to the node; and LOCAL_MAG_ROUTING_SUPPORTED, which says the gateway can route packets directly between mobile nodes anchored to the same gateway, without reverse tunnelling through the LMA. When the HAAA clears a bit in the returned vector, it is withholding that permission.
sections.plainLanguage: Each piece of information in the exchange has a named field, called an attribute value pair, with a numeric code. The codes below are the ones this RFC adds. The feature vector is the part that carries permissions: each bit says the sender supports one feature, and the server can clear a bit to say no.

sections.title: Session Management
sections.content:
For a PMIPv6 mobility session, the HAAA, the MAG and the LMA Diameter entities should be stateful and maintain the Authorization Session State Machine defined in RFC 3588. When state is maintained, a PMIPv6 mobility session identified by any of the Binding Cache Entry lookup keys described in RFC 5213 must map to a single Diameter Session-Id. If the domain separates sessions further, for example by combining the lookup keys with the service selection, then a single Diameter Session-Id must map to the PMIPv6 mobility session identified by the lookup keys and the selected service.

When both the MAG-to-HAAA and the LMA-to-HAAA interfaces are deployed and state is maintained on both, one PMIPv6 mobility session has two distinct Diameter sessions at the HAAA. The HAAA needs to be aware of this deployment possibility and should allow multiple Diameter sessions for the same PMIPv6 mobility session.

Four commands handle the end of a session, all taken from RFC 3588. The LMA or the MAG may send a Session-Termination-Request to say that the termination of an ongoing PMIPv6 session is in progress. The HAAA answers with a Session-Termination-Answer. The HAAA may send an Abort-Session-Request to the LMA or the MAG to request termination of a PMIPv6 session, and the LMA or the MAG replies with an Abort-Session-Answer. The actual PMIPv6 session termination procedures take place at the PMIPv6 protocol level and are described in RFC 5213.
sections.plainLanguage: The server, the gateway and the anchor each keep track of the sessions they are part of, and each session gets a Diameter session identifier. Because a session spans two links, the server may end up holding two Diameter sessions for one mobility session, and it has to allow that. Four commands tell the server a session is ending or ask it to end one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC applies the security considerations of the Diameter Base protocol in RFC 3588, the Diameter EAP application in RFC 4072, the Diameter NASREQ application in RFC 4005, and the Diameter Mobile IPv6 integrated scenario bootstrapping in RFC 5447.

In general, Diameter messages may travel between the LMA and the Diameter server through one or more AAA brokers or Diameter agents. In that case the LMA's communication with the Diameter server relies on the security properties of those intermediate brokers and agents, such as proxies.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC adds no security mechanism of its own. It inherits the security rules of the Diameter protocols it uses, and it notes that when a broker or proxy sits between the anchor and the server, the security of that link depends on the broker.

messages.label: L2 attach
messages.note: The device reaches the access network.

messages.label: EAP/req-identity
messages.note: The gateway asks the device for its identity.

messages.label: DER + MAG-to-HAAA AVPs
messages.note: The gateway starts the EAP exchange with the home server.

messages.label: DEA (EAP success) + MAG-to-HAAA AVPs
messages.note: The server confirms the exchange and returns the policy profile.

messages.label: PMIPv6 PBU
messages.note: The gateway asks the anchor to set up the mobility session.

messages.label: AAR + LMA-to-HAAA AVPs
messages.note: The anchor asks the home server to authorize the request.

messages.label: AAA + LMA-to-HAAA AVPs
messages.note: The server authorizes the session and returns the assigned address.

messages.label: PMIPv6 PBA
messages.note: The anchor confirms the binding to the gateway.

messages.label: RA
messages.note: The gateway sends the router advertisement to the device.

items.label: Mobile-Node-Identifier
items.desc: The mobile node identifier in NAI format.

items.label: Service-Configuration
items.desc: A grouped attribute holding a service and the LMA that hosts it.

viz.caption: Capability bits added to the MIP6-Feature-Vector attribute

items.label: PMIP6_SUPPORTED
items.desc: The gateway supports PMIPv6; the server echoes the bit to say it does too.

items.label: IP4_HOA_SUPPORTED
items.desc: The gateway can deliver an IPv4 home address to the mobile node.

items.label: LOCAL_MAG_ROUTING_SUPPORTED
items.desc: The gateway can route packets directly between mobile nodes anchored to it.
